picks.title: AI-designed proteins enable a new generation of RNA transporters
picks.excerpt: A team combined functional protein building blocks with a generative-AI-designed structural scaffold to build STV-C8, an RNA delivery vehicle. In cell culture STV-C8 delivered RNA cargo more efficiently than the virus-like particles and lipid nanoparticles tested, and in pigs it carried CRISPR/Cas9 into muscle tissue without observable toxicity.
picks.rationale: A generative-AI scaffold turned into a working RNA delivery vehicle that beat lipid nanoparticles in cell culture and carried CRISPR into pig muscle — protein design crossing from prediction into a usable tool.

picks.title: War drama Pressure depicts D-day's weather forecast—what we found when we recreated the challenge using modern systems
picks.excerpt: Andrew Charlton-Perez and Ed Hawkins re-ran the D-Day forecast with ECMWF's AIFS machine-learning forecasting system using newly digitised 1944 observations. The AI captured the North Sea storm and would have supported delaying the invasion from June 5 to June 6, but it underestimated the wind and cloud on June 6 — expert interpretation still mattered.
picks.rationale: A concrete, legible test of what an AI weather model can and cannot do: ECMWF's AIFS re-forecasting D-Day would have gotten the decision right but the severity wrong.

picks.title: In a third of cases, AI chatbots wrongly reassure sleep apnea patients that their symptoms aren't serious
picks.excerpt: Researchers ran 700 simulated consultations across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek and Grok with fictional obstructive sleep apnea patients. Correct specialist referral advice fell to 64% when the patient downplayed symptoms, and to 22-32% in the most severe cases, with chatbots offering lifestyle tips instead. Presented at the European Respiratory Society Congress.
picks.rationale: 700 simulated consultations put a number on chatbot sycophancy: correct referral advice collapses from 100% to 22-32% when the patient downplays symptoms.

picks.title: Why scientists are looking to provoke disagreement among AI brain models
picks.excerpt: Columbia University researchers synthesise 'controversial stimuli' — images engineered to make competing computational brain models disagree — then show them to people to see which model matches human perception. The method indicated the visual system blends fast discriminative computation with generative modelling rather than relying on one mechanism.
picks.rationale: Instead of scoring models on accuracy, Columbia synthesises images that force competing brain models to disagree — a method shift for deciding which model is actually right.

picks.title: BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?
picks.excerpt: Ai2 applied multidimensional item response theory across 100 LLMs and more than 34,000 benchmark questions to audit what evaluations actually measure. Safety and general reasoning emerged as the two dominant latent dimensions, and the method can cut evaluation sets by 90% while preserving predictive accuracy.
picks.rationale: Ai2 audits what LLM benchmarks actually measure across 100 models and 34,000 questions, and shows evaluation sets can shrink 90% without losing signal.
